paragraphs: A robot policy trained across many tasks can provide a starting point for learning new tasks within its existing domain. Adaptation often uses demonstrations of expert behavior. When several tasks need improvement, however, the demonstration budget creates a second problem: deciding which tasks deserve examples and how frequently to request them.

Active Multi-task Fine-tuning, or AMF, makes this allocation interactive. The agent adaptively chooses tasks for demonstration, seeking examples that provide the greatest information gain about the expert policy. This connects data collection to what the policy still needs to learn, with the objective of improving performance across tasks under a limited budget.

The paper derives performance guarantees under regularity assumptions and reports effective fine-tuning of neural policies in complex, high-dimensional environments. The theoretical result is conditional on those assumptions. The empirical findings support the practical value of treating demonstration selection as part of learning, rather than viewing the available demonstrations as a fixed input.
icml-2025-active-fine-tuning-of-multi-ta.tldr: AMF adaptively selects which tasks receive expert demonstrations to improve multi-task robot policies under a limited demonstration budget.

paragraphs: High-dimensional time series contain relationships across time that may be shared across individuals or specific to one individual. Variational autoencoders with Gaussian process priors can model such correlations, but their cubic computational cost makes scaling difficult. Existing inducing-point approximations help, although optimizing them becomes challenging when covariates include discrete values.

The paper proposes a basis function approximation for these Gaussian process priors. Its stated computational complexity is linear, addressing the scaling problem while supporting the modeling of temporal correlations. It also uses a global parametrization that removes the need for amortized variational inference and eliminates the associated amortization gap.

These design choices make the method relevant to conditional generation, where generated outputs must reflect supplied conditions while remaining computationally manageable. Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report improved scalability, interpretability, and substantially better predictive performance. The contribution therefore combines a different approximation strategy with a different inference parametrization, targeting both the computational burden and the quality of predictions.
icml-2025-bayesian-basis-function-approx.tldr: A basis function approximation makes Gaussian process prior VAEs scale linearly while improving reported prediction quality and interpretability.

paragraphs: Generating many new molecules leaves a difficult selection problem: identifying which candidates look suitable for further drug development. Existing drug-likeness predictors often depend on uncertain definitions of non-drugs or use only molecular structure. BounDr.E approaches this problem by learning a compact region around approved drugs.

The method first enriches its chemical representation by aligning it with biomedical knowledge. It then adjusts a one-class boundary through an iterative process resembling Expectation-Maximization. During this process, compounds judged insufficiently drug-like are pushed outside the boundary, progressively tightening the region used to recognize drug-like molecules.

The reported evaluation shows a 10% F1-score improvement over the previous state of the art and robust performance across datasets, including zero-shot filtering of toxic compounds. Case studies also examine large-scale computational screening. These findings support the method as a candidate-screening approach: its central contribution is combining biomedical context with an adaptive boundary around approved drugs to improve drug-likeness classification.
icml-2025-boundr-e-predicting-drug-liken.tldr: BounDr.E combines biomedical knowledge with an adaptive boundary around approved drugs to improve drug-likeness prediction.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observations becomes harder when a time series changes its behavior over time. Traditional approaches often restrict attention to fully observed variables, stationary data, or both. This paper studies a broader setting in which apparent nonstationarity can be explained by underlying, unobserved state variables.

Its key modeling condition is conditional stationarity: once the latent state is accounted for, the relevant behavior is stationary. State-Dependent Causal Inference, or SDCI, uses this structure to recover causal dependencies that depend on the state. The paper provides an identifiability result for these state-dependent causal structures, giving a theoretical basis for their recovery within the proposed setting.

Experiments on nonlinear particle interactions and gene regulatory networks report better causal discovery than baseline methods. On NBA player movements, SDCI also improves modeling results over non-causal recurrent neural networks. Together, these findings connect the structural recovery problem to forecasting, supporting the potential usefulness of causal modeling when changing behavior has the conditional structure the method assumes.
icml-2025-causal-discovery-from-conditio.tldr: SDCI discovers state-dependent causal relationships in nonstationary time series whose behavior becomes stationary when conditioned on latent states.

paragraphs: Tasks such as code generation and symbolic mathematics require answers that follow formal rules and have the right meaning. Constrained decoding can enforce a grammar, but restrictive grammars may interfere with a language model's reasoning. The paper explains theoretically why allowing only syntactically valid final answers can reduce reasoning capability.

Its central theoretical result concerns expanding the grammar with carefully designed additional rules. The authors show that such an expansion can always preserve the model's reasoning capabilities while ensuring syntactic and semantic correctness within their theoretical treatment. This motivates CRANE, a decoding algorithm that augments constrained generation with room for reasoning.

Experiments across multiple open-source models and benchmarks report improvements over both existing constrained decoding strategies and ordinary unconstrained decoding. On GSM-symbolic and FOLIO, gains reach up to 10 percentage points in accuracy. These findings support the practical importance of grammar design: constraints should accommodate the reasoning process as well as specify the form of the eventual answer.
icml-2025-crane-reasoning-with-constrain.tldr: CRANE adds reasoning-supporting grammar rules to constrained decoding, improving symbolic reasoning accuracy while retaining formal output constraints.

paragraphs: Causal structure learning seeks a directed graph without cycles that describes causal relationships among variables. Prior knowledge can concern an ancestral relationship: one variable influences another through a directed path, potentially involving intermediate variables. Incorporating this kind of knowledge into differentiable graph learning is the problem addressed here.

The paper identifies two obstacles. Relaxed mathematical descriptions of whether a path exists are not necessarily equivalent, which complicates how constraints are represented. Optimization can also violate ordering requirements among paths. The proposed framework addresses these problems with a binary-masked characterization of path relationships and an optimization strategy guided by order.

The authors provide theoretical justification for the correctness of their approach and evaluate it on synthetic and real-world datasets. The contribution is a framework for expressing and enforcing abstract causal knowledge during learning. This matters because knowledge about ancestry contains information beyond individual edges, and using it requires a representation and optimization procedure that respect the intended path constraints.
icml-2025-differentiable-structure-learn.tldr: The paper introduces a theoretically justified framework for incorporating ancestral path constraints into differentiable causal graph learning.

paragraphs: Contrastive learning commonly forms negative pairs by taking an anchor image and another image from the dataset. Different images can nevertheless share similar meaning. Treating these pairs as negatives pushes their representations apart even though their semantic relationship suggests they should remain close. The paper focuses on identifying these false negatives during training.

GloFND learns a separate detection threshold for each anchor through optimization. The thresholds are learned as training proceeds, making false-negative discovery part of the ongoing learning process. Its detection scope covers the whole dataset, extending beyond methods that identify false negatives only within the current mini-batch.

The method combines this global scope with a per-iteration computational cost that does not depend on dataset size. That pairing matters because it connects broader false-negative discovery with a scalable training step. Experiments on image and image-text data demonstrate the method's effectiveness, supporting adaptive, anchor-specific thresholds as a way to address semantically misleading negative pairs.
icml-2025-discovering-global-false-negat.tldr: GloFND learns anchor-specific thresholds during training to detect false negatives across a dataset with dataset-size-independent per-iteration cost.

paragraphs: Accuracy does not fully describe how a model behaves under adversarial attack, especially when reliable uncertainty estimates matter. This paper connects adversarial training with conformal prediction, examining both how an attacker can undermine prediction efficiency and how a defender can train against that pressure. Uncertainty becomes a central target of the analysis.

The proposed attack, OPSA, aims to maximize model uncertainty and thereby reduce conformal prediction efficiency at any significance level. Its construction does not require coverage guarantees. The corresponding defense, OPSA-AT, incorporates this attack into a new conformal training framework, making the uncertainty-focused attack part of the model's training process.

Experiments report that OPSA creates greater uncertainty than baseline attacks across various defenses. Models trained with OPSA-AT show improved robustness against OPSA and other adversarial attacks while maintaining reliable predictions in the evaluations. The findings support combining uncertainty-aware evaluation with adversarial training, extending the focus beyond whether an attacked model simply returns the correct class.
icml-2025-enhancing-adversarial-robustne.tldr: OPSA attacks conformal prediction efficiency by increasing uncertainty, while OPSA-AT uses that attack to improve empirical adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks which alternative is best while spending as few experiments as possible. In the fixed-confidence setting, an algorithm decides when to stop based on the data and must meet a correctness guarantee. Its stopping time is therefore random, making unusually long runs an important part of its behavior.

The paper shows that common stopping-time guarantees can leave this behavior insufficiently controlled. Expectation bounds can allow heavy tails, while high-probability bounds can even permit a nonzero chance of never stopping. The authors prove that this never-stopping event can occur for some popular algorithms and develop alternatives with exponentially decaying stopping-time tails.

One construction combines Sequential Halving with a doubling strategy. A second is a general transformation that accepts a fixed-confidence algorithm with a high-probability stopping guarantee and produces one with an exponential tail. These results strengthen control over rare, prolonged runs, showing why average or high-probability experiment counts alone do not fully capture the timeliness of active experimentation.
icml-2025-fixing-the-loose-brake-exponen.tldr: The paper constructs best-arm identification algorithms with exponentially decaying stopping-time tails, addressing rare prolonged or never-ending runs.

paragraphs: Metric embedding maps objects into a space where their pairwise distances are approximately preserved. This paper studies embeddings into ℓp spaces when the original distances come from a graph. The graph changes through edge insertions and deletions, so the embedding must be maintained as those updates alter its underlying metric.

The authors present what they identify as the first fully dynamic algorithm for this problem. Its guarantees jointly describe expected distance distortion, update time, and query time. An integer parameter q of at least two controls the bounds, letting the analysis expose the relationship between computational cost and distance preservation.

The stated update time is O(m^(1/q + o(1))), while query time is O(q log(n) log(nW)). Expected distortion has the bound O(log(n))^(2q) O(log(nW))^(q−1). Increasing q reduces the leading exponent in the update bound while increasing the stated distortion and query bounds. The contribution is therefore a theoretical way to maintain approximate geometric representations under graph changes, with an explicit parameter governing these competing costs.
icml-2025-fully-dynamic-embedding-into-e.tldr: The paper introduces a fully dynamic graph-metric embedding algorithm with explicit trade-offs among expected distortion, update time, and query time.

paragraphs: Offline hierarchical reinforcement learning must build useful behavior from existing trajectories. Longer tasks make selecting intermediate goals harder, especially when a successful route requires combining transitions from different recorded trajectories. Graph-Assisted Stitching, or GAS, treats this selection problem as graph search instead of learning an explicit high-level policy.

GAS embeds states in a Temporal Distance Representation and groups semantically similar states from different trajectories into shared graph nodes. This creates opportunities to connect useful transitions across recordings. A shortest-path algorithm selects a sequence of subgoals through the graph, and a low-level policy learns how to reach those subgoals.

The framework also introduces Temporal Efficiency, a metric used to remove noisy or inefficient transition states and improve the graph. Evaluations report better performance than prior offline hierarchical methods across locomotion, navigation, and manipulation. In the task most dependent on stitching, GAS scores 88.3 versus the previous state-of-the-art score of 1.0, illustrating the substantial benefit reported when combining disconnected experience is especially important.
icml-2025-graph-assisted-stitching-for-o.tldr: GAS uses graph search to stitch transitions across recorded trajectories and choose subgoals for offline hierarchical reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Synthetic video datasets commonly imitate situations that could occur in the real world. Impossible Videos asks what happens when models encounter instructions or scenes that deliberately violate that world. It separates two questions: whether video generators can create the requested impossible content, and whether video understanding models can interpret it.

The authors introduce IPV-Bench, organized into four domains and fourteen categories. Its scenes challenge physical, biological, geographical, or social laws. A prompt suite tests generation, emphasizing whether models follow unusual instructions and produce the requested creative content. A separate curated video benchmark evaluates how Video-LLMs understand impossible events.

Understanding these scenes requires reasoning about events over time and drawing on world knowledge to interpret their impossibility. The evaluations reveal limitations in current video models and identify directions for further development. The benchmark's contribution is to make impossible content a structured evaluation target, expanding assessment beyond models' ability to reproduce or recognize familiar real-world scenarios.
icml-2025-impossible-videos-4be106c5f5.tldr: IPV-Bench evaluates whether video models can generate and understand scenes that violate physical, biological, geographical, or social laws.

paragraphs: Language model alignment often aims to make a sampled answer preferable to one from a base model. Deployment increasingly uses procedures such as best-of-N sampling, controlled decoding, or tree search. The paper shows that optimizing for standard sampling can be suboptimal when a different inference procedure determines which answer reaches the user.

InfAlign targets win rate after the inference procedure has been applied. The authors prove that, for any inference-time decoding procedure, the optimal aligned policy can be obtained through a standard RLHF problem with a transformed reward. Their InfAlign-CTRL algorithm implements this idea through reward calibration followed by transformed-reward maximization with KL regularization.

For best-of-N sampling and best-of-N jailbreaking, the paper proposes specific reward transformations and reports inference-time win-rate improvements of up to 3–8%. It also finds reward calibration to be a strong baseline for ordinary win-rate optimization. The results connect alignment objectives to deployment behavior, showing that the answer-selection procedure belongs in the training objective.
icml-2025-infalign-inference-aware-langu.tldr: InfAlign transforms alignment rewards to account for deployment-time decoding, improving reported win rates for best-of-N procedures.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction constructs sets of possible labels with coverage guarantees. A marginal guarantee describes coverage for a randomly selected test point, but it can conceal differences across subpopulations. Kandinsky conformal prediction addresses how to provide more flexible conditional coverage guarantees for groups defined using both input features and labels.

The framework allows groups to overlap and permits fractional membership, so a point need not belong entirely to just one disjoint category. This expands beyond the disjoint grouping used by Mondrian conformal prediction. It also brings covariate-based group coverage, class-conditional coverage, and Mondrian methods together as special cases.

The paper establishes a minimax-optimal conditional coverage bound that holds with high probability and evaluates the approach on real-world datasets. Its theoretical contribution is a coverage bound for this richer grouping structure. Its practical significance is the ability to represent intersecting or partial memberships when assessing reliability, making the grouping scheme more expressive than a partition into separate categories.
icml-2025-kandinsky-conformal-prediction.tldr: Kandinsky conformal prediction extends conditional coverage guarantees to overlapping and fractional groups defined jointly by features and labels.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations model how a time series evolves continuously. Existing approaches often concentrate on dynamics visible in the observed states. KoNODE aims to capture a deeper source of changing behavior by explicitly allowing the parameters of the differential equation themselves to evolve over time.

The framework organizes this modeling into three levels: observed state dynamics, parameter dynamics, and underlying linear dynamics represented through Koopman operators. The evolving parameters encode information beyond the observed state trajectory, while the Koopman component captures simple intrinsic dynamics that drive the more complex behavior at the surface.

The paper links the linear dynamics to better long-term prediction and the evolving equation parameters to improved generalization to new data. Experiments on synthetic complex dynamical systems and real-world datasets demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is this hierarchical treatment of change: the model represents both how observed states move and how the parameters governing that movement evolve, using a linear dynamical component at the deepest level.
icml-2025-konode-koopman-driven-neural-o.tldr: KoNODE combines evolving differential-equation parameters with Koopman linear dynamics to improve long-term time-series prediction and generalization.

paragraphs: Vision-language models process images through multiple encoder layers before producing responses. This paper finds that harmful information is unevenly distributed across those intermediate layers. Skipping certain layers and leaving the image encoder early can increase the likelihood of harmful responses, revealing a vulnerability the authors call ICET.

Experiments on LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT, and Llama 3.2 show significant increases in harmful output when early exits are used. The result makes the processing path through the image encoder relevant to safety: behavior observed after the usual sequence of layers does not fully characterize behavior when intermediate representations are used instead.

To address the vulnerability, the authors modify Clipped Proximal Policy Optimization to perform layer-wise multimodal reinforcement learning from human feedback. Their method, Layer-Wise PPO, consistently reduces early-exit harmfulness across three multimodal datasets. The finding supports training that addresses safety across encoder layers, with the reported benefit specifically concerning the harmfulness introduced by early exits.
icml-2025-layer-wise-alignment-examining.tldr: Early image-encoder exits increase harmful responses in three tested vision-language models, and layer-wise PPO reduces this vulnerability.

paragraphs: Many mathematics benchmarks ask for a fixed answer, and some have become less informative because problems are simple or amenable to guessing and memorization. MathConstruct broadens evaluation to constructive proofs. These tasks require a model to produce a mathematical object satisfying specified properties, making the construction itself the answer.

The benchmark contains 127 challenging problems drawn from mathematics competitions. Constructive problems are useful for evaluation because a proposed object's properties can be checked automatically. The authors supply automated verifiers and use them to support problem variations, allowing evaluation of robustness as well as success on the original problems.

The evaluated state-of-the-art language models solve only 41% of the benchmark's problems. This result indicates that the collection remains challenging despite strong performance elsewhere in mathematics. MathConstruct's contribution is a combination of demanding construction tasks and checkable answers, enabling assessment of a broader form of mathematical reasoning while also testing how performance holds up when problems are varied.
icml-2025-mathconstruct-challenging-llm-.tldr: MathConstruct tests language models on 127 verifiable mathematical construction problems, with evaluated leading models solving only 41%.

paragraphs: Selecting promising candidates often requires judging several outcomes together. Conventional conformal selection handles a single response and scalar selection criteria, limiting its use when quality is multivariate. This paper develops Multivariate Conformal Selection, or mCS, to extend uncertainty-controlled selection to settings with multiple response dimensions.

The method introduces regional monotonicity and constructs conformal p-values using multivariate nonconformity scores. These scores support finite-sample control of the false discovery rate, which concerns the expected proportion of erroneous selections among selected candidates. Two variants implement the framework: mCS-dist uses distance-based scores, while mCS-learn learns scores through differentiable optimization.

Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets report significantly greater selection power while maintaining false discovery rate control. In practical terms, the reported improvement concerns finding more qualifying candidates while preserving the stated error criterion. The framework's value is to make multiple outcomes part of the selection procedure itself, extending conformal selection beyond its original univariate scope.
icml-2025-multivariate-conformal-selecti.tldr: Multivariate Conformal Selection improves reported selection power for multiple-response tasks while providing finite-sample false discovery rate control.

paragraphs: Graph learning tasks can depend on interactions between distant nodes, but establishing how much long-range interaction a task requires is difficult. Researchers commonly use performance on designated benchmarks as evidence of long-range capability. This paper argues that such empirical evidence needs a more robust theoretical characterization of what range means.

The authors formalize long-range interactions and introduce a range measure for operators on graphs. They validate the measure through synthetic experiments, then apply it to commonly used tasks and architectures. This provides a way to investigate the extent to which those tasks and models actually involve long-range interactions.

The contribution centers on measurement and evaluation. A formal notion of range can help connect claims about a model's capabilities to the interactions a task demands. The authors position their measure as a tool for assessing new datasets and architectures and for clarifying the long-range problem itself, supporting more principled interpretation of benchmark results.
icml-2025-on-measuring-long-range-intera.tldr: The paper formalizes graph interaction range and introduces a measure for examining long-range claims about tasks and architectures.

paragraphs: Permutation optimization problems seek an ordering of elements that optimizes an objective, and many are NP-hard. This paper studies what becomes possible when an algorithm receives predictions about the ordering in an optimal solution. Each prediction answers a local question: whether one specified element comes before another.

For a class of problems including scheduling, network design, and other graph permutation problems, the authors show that these predictions enable polynomial-time solutions with high probability. The stated condition is that predictions are correct with probability at least one-half plus epsilon. Thus, the result depends on access to predictions with an advantage over random pairwise guesses.

The algorithms also use predictions parsimoniously, making the amount of predictive information accessed part of the contribution. The result shows how limited, imperfect ordering guidance can change computational possibilities for the studied class. Its scope remains the learning-augmented setting: the high-probability polynomial-time guarantee relies on the supplied prediction model and its stated accuracy condition.
icml-2025-polynomial-time-learning-augme.tldr: For a class of NP-hard ordering problems, sufficiently accurate pairwise predictions enable polynomial-time solutions with high probability.

paragraphs: Transformers can be studied as systems that execute algorithms such as sorting or arithmetic. This paper examines attention whose weights depend entirely on position encodings. The motivation comes from parallel algorithms in which processors decide where to communicate using positional information, without basing that communication on the contents being processed.

The authors prove that positional Transformers retain the expressivity of the parallel computational models considered, with a depth overhead logarithmic in input length. They also analyze learning within the training distribution, focusing on how attention parameter norms affect sample complexity. Positional attention gives better theoretical dependence on those norms, but some tasks require additional layers.

Those extra layers can increase sample complexity, creating a trade-off between the benefits of positional attention and the depth needed to express an algorithm. Experiments further show good out-of-distribution performance on tasks whose underlying solutions rely on position. The results tie the usefulness of this attention design to algorithm structure, rather than establishing a universal learning advantage.
icml-2025-positional-attention-expressiv.tldr: Position-only attention preserves studied parallel computational expressivity, but its learning benefits can be offset by greater depth requirements.

paragraphs: Visual behavior cloning teaches robot manipulation from demonstrations. Common approaches seek better generalization through larger datasets or additional visual and textual information. This paper asks whether the representations learned from those inputs retain redundant information, and whether actively reducing that redundancy can improve the resulting policy.

The authors use mutual information to quantify and mitigate redundancy in latent representations. They then incorporate the Information Bottleneck principle into behavior cloning, giving learning a structured objective: compress information that is irrelevant while preserving features needed for the task. This makes the content retained in the representation a central design concern.

The study examines redundancy across methods, model backbones, and experimental settings. Evaluations on CortexBench and LIBERO report consistent performance improvements from incorporating the Information Bottleneck across the tested settings. The results support representation compression as a useful complement to richer inputs and larger datasets, showing practical value in controlling which information a behavior-cloning model carries forward into its learned representation.
icml-2025-rethinking-latent-redundancy-i.tldr: Applying the Information Bottleneck to behavior cloning reduces irrelevant representation content and consistently improves performance in the reported benchmark settings.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the precision used to store a language model's weights, helping address its substantial deployment costs. At very low precision, however, model performance can deteriorate. Existing methods also tend to offer a restricted set of bit levels, with substantial manual tuning needed for particular configurations.

SKIM combines scaled K-means clustering with mixed precision. A greedy algorithm approximately optimizes how bits are allocated across weight channels. A trainable scaling vector complements the non-differentiable clustering procedure. Together, these techniques aim to improve the quality retained after quantization while adapting to a requested bit budget.

The reported evaluation finds that SKIM narrows the perplexity gap between quantized LLaMA models and their full-precision counterparts by around 14% on average. This is a reduction in that gap, rather than a claim of a 14% improvement on every task. The contribution connects flexible precision allocation with a trainable clustering adjustment, addressing both low-precision quality and the limited configuration choices of existing methods.
icml-2025-skim-any-bit-quantization-push.tldr: SKIM combines mixed-precision bit allocation and scaled clustering, narrowing the reported LLaMA quantization perplexity gap by about 14% on average.

paragraphs: Point-cloud classifiers can face corrupted inputs whose distribution differs from their training data. Test-time training adapts models to these changes, but backpropagation during adaptation can be expensive. SMART-PC addresses both robustness and adaptation speed by combining geometric representation learning with lightweight updates at test time.

During pre-training, the model predicts skeletal representations of three-dimensional point clouds. This encourages features that capture meaningful geometric structure and are less sensitive to corruption. At test time, adaptation updates only BatchNorm statistics, avoiding backpropagation. The framework therefore links the features learned before deployment to a low-cost mechanism for responding to changed inputs.

Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ShapeNet-C, and ScanObjectNN-C report state-of-the-art classification results and better computational efficiency than existing methods, including MATE. The authors also report real-time adaptation at high frame rates. These findings support the combination of skeletal supervision and statistics-only adaptation as a way to improve corruption resilience while keeping test-time computation lightweight.
icml-2025-smart-pc-skeletal-model-adapta.tldr: SMART-PC learns skeletal point-cloud features and adapts only BatchNorm statistics, improving reported corruption robustness and efficiency without test-time backpropagation.

paragraphs: Medical visual question answering often emphasizes recognizing visible patterns or answering basic image questions. This paper introduces a benchmark aimed at more complex clinical reasoning and decision-making. It uses MRI and clinical data related to Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy, supplemented with expert annotations and insights.

The authors build clinical question-answer pairs and MRI interpretations that cover diagnosis, interpretation, and prediction of neurocognitive outcomes. Evaluations show that current large vision-language models have limited performance on this benchmark. The tasks therefore expose difficulties that extend beyond recognizing what is present in an image to reasoning about its clinical significance.

The proposed Clinical Graph of Thoughts model combines medical domain knowledge and clinical reasoning processes with vision-language interpretation. It achieves around a 15% absolute gain on the neurocognitive outcome task, which the authors identify as the most important task. This promising improvement accompanies substantial remaining challenges on the benchmark, making the work both an evaluation resource and an initial approach to the reasoning demands it introduces.
icml-2025-visual-and-domain-knowledge-fo.tldr: A clinical MRI reasoning benchmark exposes model weaknesses, while Clinical Graph of Thoughts delivers around a 15% absolute gain on neurocognitive outcome prediction.
